read.sections.0.heading.source: A place on a sea passage
read.sections.0.heading.back: A place on a sea route

read.sections.0.text.source: Melaka is a city on the west coast of the Malay Peninsula, in today's Malaysia. It lies beside the Strait of Malacca, a narrow sea passage between the peninsula and the island of Sumatra. Ships sailing between East Asia and West Asia could pass through it. In the 1400s, Melaka was an important port ruled by a Malay sultanate. A port like this can bring local people, visiting traders, goods and ideas together. Location helps explain why traders stopped there. But geography alone does not tell us who held power, or how each community lived. Find the strait on the modern map before you look at the older map.
read.sections.0.text.note: sultanate = รัฐสุลต่าน (KEY_TERMS). 'the 1400s' = ช่วงปี 1400 throughout, following KEY_TERMS' pattern (check). Second pass, one style for centuries across the course: one century is ช่วงปี 1400 ถึง 1499 (KEY_TERMS); a run of two or more is ช่วงปี 1400 ถึง 1800 กว่า ("1400 to 1800-something": accurate to the end of the last century and keeps the English numbers for the checker); late/early is ปลายช่วงปี 700 ถึง 799 / ต้นช่วงปี 900 ถึง 999; picture labels and year labels use a dash (ช่วงปี 1400–1499). Where the English itself says '15th century' (teachers' notes, picture alt) the Thai keeps คริสต์ศตวรรษที่ 15 next to the years. ช่วงปี 1400 alone (which reads as 'around 1400') and ช่วงปีคริสต์ศักราช 700 กว่า are gone. A native speaker should confirm กว่า reads well.
read.sections.0.text.back: Melaka is a city on the west coast of the Malay Peninsula in present-day Malaysia. It is beside the Strait of Malacca, a narrow sea way between the peninsula and the island of Sumatra. Ships sailing between East Asia and West Asia could pass through this strait. In the 1400s, Melaka was an important port ruled by a Malay sultanate. A port like this could bring local people, visiting traders, goods and ideas together. Location helps explain why traders stopped there, but geography alone does not tell us who had power or how each community lived. Find the strait on the modern map first, then look at the old map.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: Melaka is a city in Malaysia. It is next to the Strait of Malacca. This strait is a narrow sea between two lands. Ships going between East and West Asia sailed through it. In the 1400s, Melaka was a Malay sultanate. A sultan ruled it. It was a busy port. Traders came with goods and ideas. The strait helps explain why ships stopped there. But it does not tell us who had power.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: Melaka is a city in Malaysia. It is next to the Strait of Malacca. This strait is a narrow sea between two lands. Ships going between East Asia and West Asia sailed through here. In the 1400s, Melaka was a Malay sultanate. A sultan was the ruler. Melaka was a busy port. Traders brought goods and ideas. The strait helps explain why ships stopped there, but it does not tell who had power.

read.sections.1.heading.source: What a heritage record tells us
read.sections.1.heading.back: What the heritage record tells us

read.sections.1.text.source: UNESCO lists Melaka and George Town as World Heritage cities. It says they grew through more than 500 years of trade and exchange between East and West. It names Malay, Chinese and Indian cultures, and three European powers that ruled one after another. In 1511, Portuguese forces took Melaka. Dutch rule began in 1641, and British rule came later. The city changed over these periods. UNESCO's account is a modern heritage summary, not a diary kept by someone in Melaka in the 1400s. It helps us ask questions about long-term change. To hear one resident's view, we would need a source made closer to that person's life.
read.sections.1.text.back: UNESCO lists Melaka and George Town as World Heritage cities. UNESCO says the two cities grew from trade and exchange between East and West over more than 500 years, and mentions Malay, Chinese and Indian cultures with 3 European powers that ruled one after another. In 1511, Portuguese forces seized Melaka. Dutch rule began in 1641, and British rule followed later. The city changed in each period. UNESCO's story is a present-day heritage summary, not a diary of a person in Melaka in the 1400s. This summary helps us ask about long-term change. If we want one resident's view, we need a source made closer in time to that person's life than this.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: UNESCO says Melaka is a heritage city. People today care for its old places. UNESCO says people traded there for more than 500 years. Malay, Chinese and Indian people shaped the city. Europeans ruled it too. In 1511, the Portuguese took Melaka. In 1641, the Dutch took it. Later, the British ruled it. UNESCO wrote this in modern times. It is not a diary from the 1400s.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: UNESCO says Melaka is a heritage city. People today look after the city's old places. UNESCO says people traded there for more than 500 years. Malay, Chinese and Indian people helped build this city. Europeans also ruled this city. In 1511, the Portuguese seized Melaka. In 1641, the Dutch seized Melaka. Later the British ruled. UNESCO wrote this in the present day. It is not a diary from the 1400s.

read.sections.2.heading.source: A map from a later time
read.sections.2.heading.back: A map from a later time

read.sections.2.text.source: The second picture is a map of Melaka dated 1604, by a mapmaker named Manuel Godinho de Erédia. It comes from the Portuguese period, about 90 years after the Portuguese took the city. The map shows a large fort, a river and roads, with Portuguese labels. Some places around the fort have names, but we see few homes or people at work. A map shows what its maker chose to show, from his perspective. It is not a photo. So the map can help us study Melaka in the Portuguese period. It cannot show us what the sultanate's city looked like a century before.
read.sections.2.text.back: The second picture is a map of Melaka dated 1604 by a mapmaker named Manuel Godinho de Erédia. This map is from the Portuguese period, about 90 years after the Portuguese seized the city. The map shows a large fort, a river and streets, with labels in Portuguese. Some places around the fort have names, but we see only a few houses or working people. A map shows what its maker chose to show from his point of view. A map is not a photo. So this map helps us study Melaka in the Portuguese period, but cannot show what the sultanate's city looked like a century before.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: The second picture is an old map. It is dated 1604. That was about 90 years after the Portuguese came. The map shows a big fort and a river. Its words are in Portuguese. We see few homes or workers. A map shows the perspective of the person who drew it. It shows what he chose to draw. So this map tells us about Melaka in 1604. It does not show the city in the 1400s.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: The second picture is an old map. The map is dated 1604. By then the Portuguese had been there about 90 years. The map shows a big fort and a river. The words on the map are in Portuguese. We see very few houses and working people. The map shows the view of the person who drew it. The map shows what he chose to draw. So this map tells about Melaka in 1604, but does not show the city in the 1400s.

watch.summary.source: This is a short film by UNESCO and NHK, a TV company in Japan. It is about Melaka and George Town, two old cities by the Strait of Malacca. UNESCO's notes on the film say that people traded in the two cities for more than 500 years. Goods and ideas moved between East and West. People from Asia and Europe shaped the cities and left a mixed heritage. The notes say Melaka's old buildings show the early part of this history. UNESCO says this history began with the Malay sultanate in the 1400s. Then the Portuguese and the Dutch ruled, from the early 1500s. As you watch, remember that the film was made in our time. It shows buildings that are still standing, not people from the 1400s.
watch.summary.back: This is a short film by UNESCO and NHK, a television company in Japan, about Melaka and George Town, two old cities by the Strait of Malacca. UNESCO's record about the film says people traded in these two cities for more than 500 years. Goods and ideas travelled back and forth between East and West. People from Asia and Europe built the cities together and left a mixed heritage. The record says Melaka's old buildings show this early history. UNESCO says this history begins with the Malay sultanate in the 1400s; then the Portuguese and Dutch ruled from the early 1500s. While watching, remember that this film was made in our time. It shows buildings still standing, not people from the 1400s.

sensitiveNotes.0.note: Conquest wording kept neutral: พิชิต (conquest) for 1511, เข้ายึด for 1641, สนธิสัญญา for 1824, as in the English.
sensitiveNotes.0.back: The Portuguese conquest of Melaka in 1511 and the Dutch seizure in 1641 involved fighting, while British rule came from a treaty in 1824. The lesson states these changes of ruler directly without battle details; keep it that way. Do not ask learners about their own or their family's history, home country, religion or ethnicity. When learners think about residents' points of view, name sources to look for, not personal stories.

educatorNotes.0.source: Aim: learners explain how Melaka's place on a sea passage helped trade, and name a clear limit of a later map. Evidence move: point to the date 1604 on the map and its caption before asking anything about the 15th-century sultanate. A sound answer says location helps explain a port, and that the later map has an explicit limit. Misconception to address: the map was not drawn during the sultanate, and a modern UNESCO summary and a 1604 map are two different kinds of source.
educatorNotes.0.back: Goal: learners can explain how Melaka's location on sea routes helped trade, and give a clear limit of a later map. Evidence skill: point to 1604 on the map and caption before asking about the sultanate of 1400–1499 (15th century). A good answer says location helps explain being a port, and that a later map has clear limits. Misconceptions to address: the map was not drawn in the sultanate period, and UNESCO's present-day summary and the 1604 map are different kinds of source.

educatorNotes.1.source: Source caveats: Melaka was one of many ports in the region, so avoid suggesting it stands for all of Southeast Asia; and peoples named in a heritage summary did not share equal power. The date 1604 comes from the Commons file page and the brief. Erédia's book named in the file's credit line, the Declaraçam de Malaca, is usually dated about 1613; an NUS Press study says one of his strait maps in it is dated 1604 but does not date this city plan. Either way the map is from the Portuguese period, long after 1511.
